services.title: Concrete Parking Lots in Kansas City | Max Paving
services.desc: Concrete Parking Lots for Kansas City businesses and facilities. Family owned since 2014, our own crews, free written proposals. Call (816) 220-7777.
paras: The hardest-working pavement on a commercial property is a small fraction of it. A loaded trash truck stops at the dumpster pad on the same wheel lines every week. Delivery trucks turn hard on the dock aprons, and every car on site funnels through the same entrance lanes. Asphalt gives under loads like that, a little at a time, until the pad is rutted and the apron has shoved out of shape. Concrete doesn't give, and that difference is most of the argument for a concrete lot. Built on a properly compacted base, the areas that take the worst abuse become the ones you stop thinking about.

A full concrete lot isn't always the right answer. Much of our commercial work mixes the two materials on one site. We pour concrete where trucks stop and turn, then pave the stall areas in asphalt, because a parked car is about the lightest duty a pavement sees. Years later the asphalt sections can be overlaid without touching the concrete. Walking the site costs you nothing, and when two layouts are in play the proposal carries a separate price for each, so you're weighing real numbers instead of a hunch.

How a commercial slab ages is mostly decided on paper, before any concrete is ordered. We lay out sawcut joints from the slab thickness, keep panels near square, and avoid re-entrant corners at islands and drain inlets so the cracking follows the joints instead of wandering across panels. Reinforcement gets matched to traffic, with plain jointed panels where cars park and thicker or steel-reinforced sections under aprons and dumpster pads. ADA belongs in the design stage too, because the slope limits at accessible parking and along the path to the entrance are set by the grading plan, not the paint.
faqs: We can't close during construction. How does that work?

In stages. We keep a route open to your doors and receiving, pour one portion of the lot at a time, and don't move on until the finished section is back in service. Fresh panels can't carry a car for days after the pour, so the sequence gets built around cure windows rather than crew convenience. You get a phasing map before work starts showing which stalls close on which days, and we schedule the loudest, dustiest parts for whatever hours hurt you least.
Is a concrete lot worth the higher price compared to asphalt?

Sometimes, and it mostly depends on how long you plan to own the property. Figure 25 to 30 years or more for a concrete lot against 15 to 20 for asphalt. By the time an asphalt lot has been resurfaced and patched a few times, a concrete lot poured the same year is usually still on its original surface. Spread over decades of ownership, concrete's cost per year often comes out even or ahead. If you expect to sell within a few years, asphalt's lower first cost probably serves you better.
What maintenance does a concrete parking lot actually need?

Mostly joint care. The sawcuts get filled with a flexible sealant that keeps water and grit out of the joints. That sealant hardens and pulls away over time, and once water works under a panel through an open joint, freeze-thaw cycles and traffic start rocking and settling the slab. Have the joints checked every couple of years and plan on resealing every five to ten years depending on exposure. It is a small job next to replacing settled panels, which is where neglected joints end up.
Does concrete parking lot work stop for the winter?

The pours mostly do. Concrete needs unfrozen subgrade and a run of workable temperatures, and KC winters only offer those in stretches. Demolition, grading, and base work can keep going in colder weather than finishing can, which is why winter starts sometimes make sense for phased jobs. The tear-out and base repair get done through the cold months, and each section sits ready for concrete as soon as the thermometer cooperates.

services.name: Concrete Sidewalks
services.title: Concrete Sidewalks in Kansas City | Max Paving
services.desc: Concrete Sidewalks for Kansas City homes and businesses. Family owned since 2014, our own crews, free written proposals. Call (816) 220-7777.
paras: A raised sidewalk edge is a trip hazard, and for an HOA or a property manager it's a claim waiting to happen. A vertical offset of a quarter inch is enough to catch a toe, and when someone falls, the claim usually lands on whoever owns or maintains the walk. Most of our sidewalk work in the KC metro exists because of that exposure. We survey the walks, chalk every panel that has heaved or cracked past a safe offset, and replace only what has failed, so the hazards come off the property without paying to redo concrete that's still doing its job.

Sidewalk panels here mostly fail for one of two reasons. Tree roots lift them from below, and water moves the clay subgrade under them. A parkway tree planted a few feet off the walk decades ago has roots under it now, and a low corner that stays wet settles a little more every year. Replacing a lifted panel without dealing with the root or the drainage means replacing it again in a few years, so we look at the cause before we quote. When the offset is small and the panel is sound, grinding the edge is often the cheaper fix, and we put it on the table unprompted.

ADA compliance drives a lot of this work. Curb ramps need a compliant running slope, a cross slope under two percent, and detectable warning domes where the ramp meets the street. The same two percent limit applies to the walk itself, so a tilted panel can be out of compliance before anyone trips on it. We build ramps and accessible routes for commercial sites and HOAs, and we handle the right-of-way permits and inspections on public walks. Our curb and sidewalk work in Warrensburg, Oak Grove, and Leavenworth is public work of exactly that kind. For a board, the paperwork is half the job. Every flagged panel goes in the proposal with its location and the reason it needs work, so nobody approves a scope sight unseen.
faqs: Should we replace individual panels or the whole run?

Per-panel replacement is right when most of the walk is sound and the failures are scattered. You pay only for the panels that have moved, and the new concrete ties into the old at existing joints. A full run makes more sense when a root system or a drainage problem runs the length of the walk, or when so many panels have failed that saving the survivors costs more than finishing the job. The survey usually settles it, because the panel count makes the math plain.
What triggers ADA requirements on sidewalk work?

New construction and alterations trigger them. Replace a panel along an accessible route and the new panel needs a compliant cross slope even if the old one never had it. Rebuild a ramp and it needs current slopes and detectable warnings. Maintenance that leaves the surface in place, like grinding an edge, generally doesn't trigger an upgrade. Work in the public right-of-way follows the city's own standards. We sort out which requirements apply during the site walk so nothing shows up later as a change order.
How long before residents can walk on new panels?

Two days behind barricades is the norm; cold weather adds a day or two. Concrete spends about a month climbing to its design number, but a person walking across a panel needs only a fraction of it. On occupied properties we replace panels in a sequence that never cuts off a building entrance, barricade the fresh pours, and open sections as they cure. Residents lose a short stretch of walk for a day or two, not the whole network at once.
Do we need a city permit for sidewalk replacement?

Street-side walks almost always sit in public right-of-way, and most metro cities want paperwork before you cut into one, sometimes an inspection on both sides of the pour. Each city also writes its own spec for thickness, joints, and ramps. Chasing all of that down is our errand, not yours, and it happens before demolition gets scheduled. Walks inside a private community are usually exempt, though we check instead of assuming.

services.name: Concrete Curbs & Gutters
services.title: Concrete Curbs & Gutters in Kansas City | Max Paving
services.desc: Concrete Curbs & Gutters for Kansas City homes and businesses. Family owned since 2014, our own crews, free written proposals. Call (816) 220-7777.
paras: Curb and gutter is the drainage system at the edge of your pavement. The gutter pan catches runoff and carries it along the curb line to the storm inlets before it can soak in under the asphalt. When a section settles or the pan cracks through, that water stops moving toward the inlet and starts going into the base instead, which is why a failing curb line and a failing pavement edge usually show up together. So if the curbs around your commercial lot are cracked, tipped, or breaking apart at the gutter line, the concrete you can see is only part of the problem.

How we form the curb depends on the run. Long straight stretches get formed and poured in continuous runs so lane closures stay short. Short repairs, tight radii, transitions at catch basins, and sections that have to match an odd existing profile get hand-formed. On repair work we saw-cut the failed section out at the nearest joint, then drill and epoxy dowels into the sound concrete on both ends so the new piece is tied to the old ones instead of floating between them. An untied section settles on its own schedule, and the joint opens up.

Curb work and paving work need to be planned as one job. An overlay adds a couple inches of new asphalt, and if nobody accounts for that, the curb face shrinks by the same amount and runoff starts jumping the curb in a hard rain. When we handle both, we mill along the gutter line so the finished pavement meets the pan cleanly and the curb keeps its full reveal. On public work the city's own specs and inspections set the rules, as they have on our curb and sidewalk work in Warrensburg in 2025 and in Oak Grove and Leavenworth in 2026.
faqs: Should we replace the curb before the lot work, or as part of it?

Before the new pavement goes down, and ideally as part of the same project. The curb establishes the edge height and the drainage line, so pouring it first lets the asphalt be laid tight against the pan. Replacing curb after paving means saw-cutting into a brand new surface and patching against it. Doing both under one contract also puts one company on the hook for how the water flows when the job is finished.
How long does new curb need to cure before it can take traffic?

About seven days before it should take vehicle contact in warm weather, and cold snaps stretch that. It keeps gaining strength until full cure at 30 days. We cone off fresh sections and phase the pours so the rest of the lot stays open the whole time. A car parked against week-old curb is not a problem. Truck tires climbing over the face early are, so we plan the work around your delivery routes and keep barricades up until the concrete is ready.
Can you match the profile of our existing curb?

Yes. Most commercial curb in the KC area follows a standard barrier or curb and gutter section, and we form new work to match what is there. For odd or older profiles we take measurements off a sound section and build forms to fit. The exception is height. If a past overlay took away part of your curb face, matching that shorter profile just repeats the mistake, so expect a conversation about restoring the full face before any forms get built.
Do you do small curb repairs, or only full replacements?

Yes, small repairs are normal work for us. A tipped section at a drive entrance or a piece a plow caught can be cut out and replaced without touching the rest of the run. The judgment call is drainage. If the rest of the curb line still carries water to the inlets, spot replacement is the right money. If long stretches have settled and the pan holds water, piecemeal repair means paying mobilization over and over, and at some point the full run becomes the better spend.

services.name: Concrete Pads (HVAC, Dumpster, Equipment)
services.title: Concrete Dumpster & HVAC Pads in Kansas City | Max Paving
services.desc: Concrete dumpster, HVAC, and equipment pads for Kansas City properties, poured level on a compacted base. Free written proposals: (816) 220-7777.
paras: Most dumpster pads we pour are replacing asphalt that has already been patched at the enclosure more than once, held a season, and failed again. The reason is the truck. A loaded front-load garbage truck can run over 50,000 pounds, and when it lifts the container over the cab, much of that weight shifts onto the front axle, stopped in the same spot several mornings a week. Asphalt is designed with give in it, and that give turns into ruts and ridges when the load never varies and never moves. The fix is a reinforced concrete pad under the enclosure, built to take that axle without moving.

We size a dumpster pad for the enclosure plus the approach apron, the ten to fifteen feet where the truck actually stands during service. Bollards, gate posts, and the enclosure itself get planned around the pour rather than drilled in afterward. We also look at the drive lane leading in. A truck that crosses tired asphalt to reach a new pad will start breaking the lane next, and sometimes the right scope includes a section of it. Sometimes it doesn't, and the proposal simply won't include it.

HVAC and equipment pads are a different job with different rules. A condenser or generator carries a steady static load, so the spec is lighter, and what matters more is a level surface, a base compacted so the unit won't settle out of level, and room around it for service access. Transformer and heavier equipment pads fall in between and get sized to what's sitting on them. A dumpster pad is the opposite, and the piece that decides how long it lasts is the approach apron. Most of the failed pads we replace stopped at the enclosure gate, leaving the front wheels to take every lift on asphalt.
faqs: Why does the asphalt at my dumpster enclosure keep failing no matter how many times it's patched?

Because a patch is more of the same material carrying the same abuse, bonded to broken pavement at its edges, so each one starts life weaker than the surface around it and fails a little sooner. The truck, the route, and the spot where it stops never change, so the outcome won't either until the material under the wheels does. A rigid pad spreads the axle load into the base instead of deforming, and that ends the cycle.
How thick does a dumpster pad need to be, and what goes in it?

Six to eight inches for a pad taking truck service, depending on the trucks and pickup frequency. We reinforce with a rebar grid rather than wire mesh, since mesh usually ends up at the bottom of the slab doing nothing. What's under the concrete matters as much as what's in it, so the subgrade gets compacted and an aggregate base goes down before forming. An HVAC or equipment pad is a lighter spec, typically four inches, since the load is static and measured in hundreds of pounds rather than tons.
How long is the dumpster off the pad while the concrete cures?

About 7 days with a standard mix, or 2 to 3 days with a faster-curing mix that costs more. Cold weather stretches both. The concrete keeps gaining strength for about a month, but a pad designed for truck loads doesn't need every bit of that before the container comes back, and we'll give you a specific return date for your pour instead of a guess. Before demo starts we coordinate with your hauler on a temporary container location so trash service continues through the project. That call is worth making early, since some haulers want a few days of notice.
Will a new pad throw off the drainage in the rest of the lot?

Not if it's built to the existing flow lines. Before forming anything we shoot grades on the surrounding asphalt and set the pad so water keeps moving the way the lot already drains. A pad poured high dams water against the enclosure. A pad poured dead flat holds washdown water and dumpster runoff, which turns to ice in winter. We slope the pad, usually one to two percent, toward the lot's existing flow path and match the asphalt edge so trucks don't catch a lip.

services.name: Heavy-Duty Concrete Truck Lanes & Warehouse Paving
services.title: Heavy-Duty Concrete Paving in Kansas City | Max Paving
services.desc: Heavy-duty concrete truck lanes, dock aprons, and warehouse paving for Kansas City facilities, designed for the loads. Free proposals: (816) 220-7777.
paras: A loaded semi concentrates its weight onto a few small contact patches, and the worst damage happens at low speed, while the truck is turning, backing into a dock, or braking in the same spots every shift. Under that kind of loading asphalt deforms. It ruts where wheels dwell, shoves into ridges at the dock doors, and breaks up under parked trailers, even when the original paving job was done well. The pavement simply was never built for what the facility puts on it. We build heavy-duty concrete truck lanes, loading zones, and trailer parking for warehouses and distribution facilities across the Kansas City metro.

Truck pavement is a different design problem than a car lot. The concrete in a lane that carries semis is thicker than what goes under passenger cars, poured over a compacted base, reinforced so the slab spans weak spots instead of breaking over them, and jointed with dowels that carry wheel loads from one panel to the next. Dock approaches and dolly pads take the most abuse, since trailer landing gear and drive axles sit motionless on one patch of slab for hours at a stretch. We size each area for the loads it will actually see, so you're not paying to pave the whole site to the heaviest spec.

We handle both new construction and remove-and-replace, and most replacement calls come from facilities that can't shut down. There's no charge to have us walk the site, and the written proposal maps which sections have failed and which are getting close. Warehouses in the Lenexa, Olathe, and KCK corridors run around the clock, and a paving schedule that ignores that is useless, so sequencing gets worked out with your operations people before anything is booked. Failed sections come out and go back a few dock positions or one stretch of lane at a time, with a truck route kept open, and the facility keeps shipping while the pavement gets replaced under it.
faqs: We ship 24/7. How does concrete replacement work around that?

The working rule is that we never demolish more concrete than we can pour and cure on the agreed schedule, so an open truck route is never hostage to a weather delay. With a standard mix, a new section typically needs about seven days before it carries a loaded trailer again, and demolition is scheduled around that reality instead of hoping. The slab keeps gaining strength until full cure at 30 days, but it is ready for use well before that. When a facility has to be running again in two or three days, a faster-curing mix gets it there. That mix costs more, so we price it as an option where the schedule calls for it.
How much thicker does truck-lane concrete need to be than a regular parking lot?

Most of our heavy-duty concrete runs 8 to 10 inches thick, and where a given lane lands in that range depends on the loads. A lane carrying loaded semis all day needs that thickness plus reinforcement and dowelled joints that a light-duty lot usually skips. What sets the spec is your traffic. Axle weights, trucks per day, and whether they're turning or braking on that section. Base, drainage, and slope get the same attention on every job, because a thick slab over a wet base still fails. We state the designed thickness and reinforcement in writing, so a lower bid has to show what it left out.
Our asphalt dock approaches rut every summer. Is concrete the fix?

Usually, yes. Dock approaches take slow, heavy traffic in the same small area, which is the exact condition asphalt handles worst and concrete handles well. We saw-cut the failed asphalt, rebuild and compact the base underneath, and pour reinforced concrete aprons tied into the surrounding pavement. The asphalt parking fields can stay, since they're fine for what they carry. Plan on each apron being out of service through demolition, the pour, and about a week of cure with a standard mix, which is why we replace them a few at a time rather than all at once.
How long will concrete truck lanes last under daily semi traffic?

Designed for the loads and poured over a sound base, decades. Twenty to thirty years is a fair expectation for a heavy-duty lane, where asphalt in the same service can rut badly within a few years. The routine upkeep is joint sealing, so water never reaches the base. What shortens concrete's life is underdesign. A slab specced for cars will crack and fault under semis no matter how well it was poured, so we ask about your truck counts before we talk numbers.

services.name: Concrete Repair & Replacement
services.title: Concrete Repair & Replacement in Kansas City | Max Paving
services.desc: Concrete Repair & Replacement for Kansas City homes and businesses. Family owned since 2014, our own crews, free written proposals. Call (816) 220-7777.
paras: Most of the concrete we get called about is 20 or 30 years old and showing it. A panel near the garage has settled, the surface is flaking off in patches, or a crack that was filled two summers ago is back and wider than before. Almost any of it can be patched. Whether the patch holds depends on what is going on underneath. A crack or two along the joints, or one dropped panel, is usually a contained problem with a contained fix. Concrete cracked in every direction, ponding water, or settling in several places at once usually means the base has failed, and a repair sitting on a failed base does not stay fixed.

Around here the damage usually starts in the ground, not the concrete. The soil under most of eastern Jackson County spends spring taking on water and late summer giving it up, and every slab on top goes along for the ride. Once a crack opens, each freeze levers it a little wider, and our winters hand out those cycles by the dozen. Spalling is different, and usually goes back to the original pour. Concrete finished with bleed water still on the surface, or batched without air entrainment, starts shedding its top layer after a few years of salt and freezing.

The fix depends on how deep the damage goes. A small spall at a joint or an edge can sometimes be cut out and patched on its own, which makes sense only when the slab under it is still sound, so that is the first thing we check. When spalling or scaling has spread across a panel, replacing the panel is usually the lasting fix. Cracks that run through the slab call for full-depth repair down to the base, and a panel that has settled or broken apart comes out whole and gets repoured. Whatever we recommend, you get the reasoning in writing along with the price, so you can weigh it without anyone standing in your driveway waiting on an answer.
faqs: How do you decide whether concrete should be repaired or replaced?

The share of the surface that has failed is the biggest factor. Damage confined to a few panels or joints on a slab that is otherwise stable is worth repairing. Once roughly a third of the surface needs work, repair pricing starts crowding replacement pricing, and replacement resets the clock on the whole slab instead of part of it. A slab that keeps cracking after earlier patches has a problem underneath, and more patching will not outrun it. We walk it and tell you which side of the line yours is on.
Will the repaired section match the rest of my concrete?

No. Concrete gets its color from the cement, the sand and rock in the mix, the finish work, and years of weathering, and a new pour can only duplicate some of that. A fresh patch reads bright against old gray, and while the contrast softens over the first few seasons it never disappears. Replacing a full panel between existing joints hides it best, because the eye already expects a change at a joint line. If a contractor promises an invisible patch, they're overselling what concrete can do.
How quickly can you get out after I call?

Most repair calls come from inside a half-hour of our Grain Valley shop, so we can usually have someone out within one to three days. The written proposal follows within a few business days of the visit. Repairs are usually smaller jobs, so they can often be scheduled sooner, and approved work often starts within a few weeks during the paving season. If a panel has become a trip hazard, tell us when you call and we will move it up.
Can you pave asphalt over our old concrete instead?

Sometimes, but we usually advise against it. Asphalt can go over existing concrete when the concrete is stable and in good enough shape that it won't damage the new surface in a couple of years. The trouble is that concrete bad enough to want covering usually isn't sound enough to pave over, and the cracks and joints underneath tend to come up through the asphalt. Most of the time, replacing the failed sections is the fix that lasts.
What makes concrete settle around Kansas City?

Uncompacted fill does a lot of it. Builders backfill against the foundation when the house goes up, that fill keeps consolidating for years, and that's why driveways so often sink right at the garage. Water does the rest. A downspout dumping beside the slab or a joint that has lost its seal washes out base material until the panel drops into the void. Repairing the concrete without correcting the water is temporary, so the proposal covers both when drainage is at fault.

services.name: Concrete Driveways
services.title: Concrete Driveways in Kansas City | Max Paving
services.desc: Concrete Driveways for Kansas City homeowners. Family owned since 2014, our own crews, free written proposals. Call (816) 220-7777.
paras: A residential concrete driveway in the Kansas City area should be poured at least four inches thick, five to six if anything heavier than a pickup will sit on it, using 4,000 PSI air-entrained concrete. The air entrainment matters in this climate. Those microscopic air pockets give freezing water somewhere to expand, which is why a good slab here survives dozens of freeze-thaw cycles a year without scaling. Reinforcement and correctly spaced control joints decide where the concrete cracks. All concrete cracks. The craft is making it crack where you planned.

Most of our driveway work is removal and replacement. We break out and haul off the old slab, look hard at the subgrade underneath, regrade and compact, add aggregate base where the soil needs it, then form, pour, finish, and cut joints. The subgrade step is where driveways in this region are won or lost. Eastern Jackson County soil takes on water in spring and gives it up in August, and a new slab over an unfixed base fails the same way the old one did.

Price comes down to square footage, thickness, how much old surface has to come out, whether the base needs rebuilding, slope and drainage, and how easily equipment can reach the site. A straight rectangular replacement costs the least per foot. Turnarounds, widenings, and decorative finishes add cost, but they're far cheaper to do during the pour than to add later. We check all of it on the site visit, and the written proposal spells out the scope so you know what the price covers.
faqs: How long before I can use my new concrete driveway?

Foot traffic after a day or two, passenger vehicles after about a week, full cure at 30 days. With a faster-curing mix, which costs more, cars can go on it in 2 to 3 days. If an RV or a loaded truck will sit on the driveway, tell us at the site visit so we pour that area thicker. Cold weather stretches those times, and we schedule and protect the pour accordingly.
Will my new driveway crack?

All concrete cracks. The goal is controlling where. Properly cut control joints give the slab straight, planned lines to crack along instead of random ones across the surface. Early random cracking is a different story, and it almost always traces back to a poor base, missing joints, or a bad mix. Our written guarantee covers that difference.
What does a concrete driveway cost in the KC metro?

It swings enough with size, tear-out, base condition, and finish that a number given blind would probably mislead you. The onsite proposal is free, and it puts the real price for your driveway in writing. As a general rule concrete costs more than asphalt up front, and spread over its lifetime it often comes out even or ahead.
Can you pour a driveway in winter?

Down to a point. Cold-weather pours use heated water or accelerators in the mix and insulated blankets during cure, and we never pour on frozen subgrade. Below about 20 degrees sustained it stops being worth the risk, and we'll say so rather than force a date. Late fall pours are routine.

services.name: Asphalt Parking Lots
services.title: Asphalt Parking Lots in Kansas City | Max Paving
services.desc: Asphalt Parking Lots for Kansas City businesses and facilities. Family owned since 2014, our own crews, free written proposals. Call (816) 220-7777.
paras: Pricing asphalt paving for a commercial property in the Kansas City area comes down to two questions, whether the building is a retail strip, an office park, a church, or a warehouse. What the lot actually needs, and whether the business can stay open while the work happens. We pave commercial lots out of Grain Valley, and the answer starts with a walk across your pavement. Some lots need a new wearing surface. Some need to come out down to the dirt. Before a number goes on paper, we'll stand out there with you and point out what the cracking is telling us.

That walk is mostly about the base. Asphalt is a flexible pavement, and it's only as strong as the compacted rock and subgrade under it. When the cracking has connected into a chicken-wire pattern, or the drive lanes have rutted and started holding water, the base has already failed, and new hot mix laid over it inherits the failure. Where the base is sound, milling and a fresh lift restores the lot for years. Where it isn't, we excavate, correct the subgrade, rebuild the rock section, and pave new. On full replacements and new construction we design the thickness for the traffic, heavier in truck lanes and at dumpster pads than in the stalls.

Almost every commercial job is phased so you never lose the whole lot at once. We split the lot into sections so entrances and fire lanes stay open, and if the constraint is Sunday services or clinic hours, the schedule bends around them. Grades at accessible parking and along the route to the door are built to current ADA slope standards. Drainage gets the same attention, because freeze-thaw winters here turn standing water into pavement damage. The site visit and written proposal are free, and it's detailed enough to hand to an owner or a board.
faqs: What drives the cost of a commercial asphalt parking lot?

Size sets the baseline, but two lots the same size can price very differently. How much old pavement has to be torn out and hauled off sets one chunk of the price. What the base turns out to need once it's exposed sets another, anywhere from a proof roll to a full rebuild. Asphalt thickness for your traffic, drainage corrections, concrete work like curbs and dumpster pads, and phasing to keep you open all add from there. The written proposal spells out the scope, so you can see what's included and talk through what could be cut or deferred.
How long will my lot be out of service?

Each work zone can usually carry traffic again the same day it's paved, once the asphalt is compacted and has cooled, often within a few hours. Keeping cars off for a day or two is better for the surface when tenants can spare it, and a July or August mat holds its heat longer, so we give you a time on paving day. Milled areas can carry cars while they wait for new pavement, which helps. A straightforward overlay on a mid-size lot often wraps in under a week. Full reconstruction runs longer because excavation and base work add days to each phase. Your proposal includes the phasing plan and dates so you can notify tenants ahead of time.
How do you decide between an overlay and full replacement?

We look for evidence of what's happening under the surface. Isolated cracks and a faded, rough top usually mean the structure is fine and an overlay will hold. When cracks have joined into whole failed sections and the surface flexes under a loaded truck, the base has quit. Most aging lots land in between, so the usual scope is surgical. We rebuild the areas that failed from below and resurface the rest, which keeps reconstruction money in your pocket.
Do you handle the concrete parts of a lot too, like curbs and dumpster pads?

Yes, and it usually belongs in the same bid. Curbs control the drainage that protects the asphalt, and dumpster pads take loads asphalt was never meant to carry, so we pour those in concrete while the paving crew handles the lot. One contractor, one schedule, one number, and nobody pointing at another trade if something needs attention later.

services.name: Asphalt Driveways
services.title: Asphalt Driveways in Kansas City | Max Paving
services.desc: Asphalt Driveways for Kansas City homeowners. Family owned since 2014, our own crews, free written proposals. Call (816) 220-7777.
paras: Cracks across the surface, crumbling edges, patches that stopped holding. When an asphalt driveway gets to that point, full replacement is usually the right call, and it's most of the residential asphalt work we do. We tear the old pavement out, haul it away, and fix what's underneath, because a soft base turns into a dip in the new surface within a couple of winters. Once the base is compacted and weak spots are built back up with rock, two to three inches of hot-mix asphalt goes down and gets rolled tight while it's still hot, which is the step bargain crews tend to rush.

Asphalt has a real advantage in Missouri weather because it flexes with the ground instead of fighting it. The clay under most Kansas City yards is always taking on water or giving it back, and the ground moves as it does. Winter here thaws and refreezes constantly, and a flexible pavement rides that movement better than a rigid slab. When damage does show up, asphalt is quick and inexpensive to repair. Asphalt also costs noticeably less than the same footprint in concrete, which matters on a long or wide driveway. The tradeoff is that asphalt asks for more attention over the years and concrete needs very little.

Most of what separates a good asphalt driveway from a cheap one lives at the edges, which is why we walk the site before quoting anything and put the full scope in a free written proposal. Unsupported edges along the yard get rolled at an angle so they hold up when a tire runs off the pavement. Where the pavement meets the garage floor, it has to land flush, or you scrape coming in and trap water at the door. And the street tie-in gets worked until you pull in without feeling the seam.
faqs: How soon can we park on a new asphalt driveway?

Usually the same day. Once the asphalt is compacted and has cooled, often within a few hours, it can take your car, but if you can give it a day or two, that's better for the surface. Heat slows the cooling, so we'll give you a time on paving day. Through the first season, be gentle with the surface. Get the car rolling before you turn the wheel, set trailer jacks and kickstands on a board, and park anything heavy somewhere else.
How long will an asphalt driveway last?

A well-built residential driveway in this climate is good for 15 to 20 years, and careful owners get more. What kills driveways early is water: open cracks that feed the base through a few winters until it moves. Keep water draining off the surface and deal with damage when it shows up, and the driveway reaches the far end of that range.
How thick should a residential asphalt driveway be?

Two to three inches of compacted hot-mix asphalt over four to six inches of compacted aggregate base is the standard for cars and pickups in this area. The base does more work than most people expect. It spreads the load and drains water away from the pavement, which is why we spend real time on it during a replacement. If you park a heavy trailer, boat, or RV, tell us at the site visit and we'll thicken the section where it sits.

services.desc: Asphalt Patch Repair for Kansas City homes and businesses. Family owned since 2014, our own crews, free written proposals. Call (816) 220-7777.
paras: There's a pothole at your entrance that keeps getting bigger, or a strip of drive lane that breaks up every year no matter what goes in it. The real question is whether the damage stops at the surface. We patch asphalt for commercial properties and homeowners across the Kansas City metro, from a few failed spots in an apartment lot to a driveway crumbling at the apron. A patch that lasts starts with saw-cut edges. We cut a clean rectangle around the failure instead of feathering into ragged pavement, remove the failed material, and tack-coat the vertical faces so the new hot mix bonds to the old asphalt instead of sitting against it.

There are two legitimate ways to patch asphalt. A surface patch removes and replaces the top couple of inches, and it's the right repair when the damage stops there, like raveling along a seam or a shallow depression that hasn't cracked through. Full-depth patching takes the asphalt out down to the base, recompacts or rebuilds whatever is soft underneath, and paves back in compacted lifts. Potholes almost always need full depth, because a pothole means water already got into the base and softened it. Throwing cold mix in from the top is the fix that comes back out by spring.

Sometimes patching is triage. If failed areas keep spreading year over year, the base under the pavement is going, and patches buy time instead of fixing the problem. Buying time can still be the right move when budget or season says wait, but you should know that's what you're buying. On commercial properties, access often matters as much as the repair. We work drive lanes in pieces so tenants and delivery trucks keep moving. A section cut out in the morning usually carries traffic again by evening.
faqs: Should I patch my asphalt or repave the whole thing?

A useful rule is how much of the pavement is failing. If the bad areas add up to a small fraction and the rest still drains and rides fine, patching makes sense. When failures are scattered everywhere, or the same spots come back every year after repair, you're paying repair prices for a replacement problem. We look at the whole surface during the visit before recommending either. Neither the visit nor the written proposal costs anything, and it says plainly which kind of job yours is.
How long does a proper asphalt patch last?

A full-depth patch over a recompacted base should last as long as the pavement around it, and on older asphalt it usually outlasts the surrounding surface. A surface patch is shorter-lived by nature, generally a few years depending on traffic and how much water moves through that spot. What kills patches early is corner-cutting you can't see once the job is rolled flat. You see it the following spring, when the edges unravel and the center sinks.
Can you match my existing asphalt?

Structurally, yes. Visually, not at first. Fresh asphalt is black and your existing pavement has grayed with age, so a new patch reads darker for a season or two before it weathers toward the color around it. We match the mix type and compact it flush, so the ride and the edges are seamless. Give it a season or two of sun and the color difference quietly disappears.
Is my job too small? Do you have a minimum?

There's no single minimum, since it depends on the type of job, but mobilization is real. Bringing a crew and hot mix to a site costs about the same whether we patch one pothole or twelve, so a single small hole carries a high price per square foot. A pothole or two on its own usually isn't worth the trip for either of us. Most small jobs make sense grouped, like fixing every failed spot on a property in one visit, and if you call about one pothole we'll tell you honestly what would make the trip worth it.

services.title: Asphalt Mill & Overlay in Kansas City | Max Paving
services.desc: Asphalt Mill & Overlay for Kansas City homes and businesses. Family owned since 2014, our own crews, free written proposals. Call (816) 220-7777.
paras: Mill and overlay sits between patching a worn asphalt surface and rebuilding it from the ground up. A milling machine grinds off the top inch and a half to two inches of old asphalt. The millings get hauled off and recycled. The exposed surface is cleaned and tack-coated, and a fresh lift of hot-mix asphalt goes down over it. You keep the base you already paid for and get a new wearing surface at a fraction of reconstruction cost.

The part that requires honesty is knowing when it works. Mill and overlay is the right call when the failure lives in the surface. Raveling, oxidation, surface cracking, minor rutting. It's the wrong call when the failure is underneath. Widespread alligator cracking, deep ruts, and sections that pump water are base failures, and an overlay on top of them buys maybe two or three years before the same pattern telegraphs through. When we evaluate your pavement we tell you which category it's in, even when the answer is the cheaper one.

Milling also solves problems a straight overlay can't. It preserves curb reveal and drainage flow lines, since paving over the top raises the surface and can trap water or bury curbs. It lets us correct grade in low spots that pond. And it gives the new lift a clean surface to bond to. On commercial lots we mill and pave in sections so tenants and customers keep parking through the project.
faqs: How do I know if my lot needs mill-and-overlay or full replacement?

The cracking pattern tells most of the story. Scattered straight cracks, a gray oxidized color, and rough texture point to overlay. Interconnected alligator cracking, ruts you can feel driving, or spots that stay wet point to base failure, which an overlay only hides for a while. We walk the lot and mark which areas are which. Many jobs end up as full-depth repair in the failed spots plus overlay across the rest, which costs far less than blanket reconstruction.
How long does a mill and overlay last?

Over a sound base, a properly built overlay typically gives a commercial lot 10 to 15 years, longer when water is kept out of the cracks and the surface is maintained. Over a failed base, two or three years. That difference is why the evaluation matters more than the quote.
Can my business stay open during the work?

Usually, yes. We phase the work in sections, milling and paving one area while the rest of the lot stays open, then rotating. New asphalt can usually take traffic the same day, once it's compacted and cooled, though a day or two is better when your schedule allows. We plan the phasing around your delivery schedules and peak hours.
Why not just pave over the old surface without milling?

Sometimes a true overlay is legitimate on a low, sound surface. But skipping the milling raises your finished grade about two inches. That can bury curbs, break drainage into catch basins, create trip lips at sidewalks and doorways, and throw off ADA slopes at accessible stalls. If someone quotes you a pave-over at a price that seems too good, ask them what happens at your curbs and doors.

Usually the same day. Once a patch is compacted and has cooled, often within a few hours, it can take cars, and commercial-grade asphalt can take trucks. A day or two is better when you can spare it, and on a hot summer day cooling takes longer, so we'll give you a time on the day of the work. Overlay my Blue Springs lot, or full replacement?

If the damage lives in the surface, meaning oxidation, raveling, and straight cracks, an overlay on your existing base is the economical fix. If there's widespread alligator cracking or areas pumping water, the base has failed and overlay money would be wasted. We walk the lot, mark the failed areas, and usually land on full-depth repair in those spots plus overlay everywhere else.
Can you fix just the failed area if the rest of the lot is fine?

Yes, and it's usually the right call. Entrances and drive lanes take the turning loads, so they fail years before the parking stalls do. We cut out and rebuild the failed area full depth and leave sound pavement alone, which keeps the bill tied to the actual problem.

faqs: Does every curb or sidewalk cut in Grain Valley need its own permit?

Past the right-of-way line, we size the rest of the driveway for what will be driving on it.
Can my downspouts and sump pump drain toward the street in Grain Valley?

A new driveway often changes where that water ends up, especially when an old downspout used to spill across the slab toward the street. We plan for drainage on every job, so if a downspout or sump line is going to dump too close to the curb or the neighbor's yard, the proposal stage is the time to bring it up and plan where it goes.

That is the least the code accepts, not what every lot needs. Where loaded trucks stop and turn, on truck lanes and dock aprons, we typically pour 8 to 10 inches of concrete depending on many factors, on a base and drainage designed around that weight.

USDA maps much of Fairfax as Onawa, a clay soil that swells and stays wet, and the Armourdale and Argentine bottoms as silty Eudora soil, which is prone to frost heave. We look at the subgrade, how the site drains, and whether the base has to be thicker or stabilized before we put a number on it.
How wide can a new driveway be in Kansas City, Kansas?

Under the Unified Government's Public Works guidance, a driveway can be up to 25 feet wide at the street and has to stay 3 feet off the property line. Hard surface can't cover more than 40 percent of the front or back yard. The permit application asks for a simple drawing showing the driveway's length, width and placement, plus a Kansas 811 locate ticket. Chapter 32 of the UG code has the full rules, and we check with Public Works for anything that has changed before the pour.
Is the higher ground near the Turner Diagonal easier to pave than the river bottoms?

Not really. The problems are just different up there. Around the Turner Logistics Center, USDA maps the ground mostly as Marshall silt loam, with some Ladoga, and both have a silty clay loam subsoil. USDA flags both for local roads, giving frost action, low strength and a subsoil that swells and shrinks as the reasons. The Kansas Geological Survey's county geology also warns that bare loess can gully in a single rainy season, so graded slopes and outfalls next to new pavement need protecting.

faqs: Is a geotechnical report required before we rebuild a truck court in Lenexa?

For new public streets, Lenexa's technical specifications require a geotechnical report sealed by a Kansas-licensed engineer or geologist, and they require the street subgrade to be treated with fly ash, cement, lime kiln dust or lime. Lenexa won't accept a public street built on untreated native soil, which is worth remembering for any lane loaded trailers will use. Whether a private truck court needs a report depends on the scope, and we confirm that with the city. If a soils report was done when your building went up, it's the first thing we'd ask to see. If the loads or the ground call for an engineered pavement design, we'll say so before you sign anything.
Will adding pavement change what we owe Lenexa for stormwater?

It might. Lenexa charges a one-time Storm Systems Development Charge at the time of construction, and for commercial and multi-family property the city figures it by dividing total impervious area by 2,750 square feet. Erosion and site development fees are assessed with land disturbance and site development permits, and a separate stormwater utility charge shows up on Johnson County property tax bills. Whether widening a truck lane on an existing site triggers any of these is a question we put to the city before you commit. Our proposal lists how many square feet of new hard surface the job adds, so the city has the number it needs to answer.
How thick does Lenexa want a drive entrance poured?

The city's 2026 technical specifications call for 6-inch concrete on residential drives and 8-inch on commercial ones, built as a concrete apron to Lenexa's standard details. The finish is non-slip, made with a wood float and then a broom or hairbrush pulled across the entrance. The concrete has to be vibrated, slump can't exceed 5 inches, and the grade has to be compacted and can't be frozen while the work is going on. Lenexa put out new editions of these specs in both 2025 and 2026, so we build to whichever edition and details are current when the permit is issued.
How far into my front yard does Lenexa's right-of-way go?

In residential areas it typically reaches 11 feet behind the curb, so the street end of most driveways sits inside it. Elsewhere it usually ends 1 foot behind the sidewalk. Work in that strip needs a city right-of-way permit, and we pull it before our crew works there. If you're not sure where your line falls, the city's permit staff at 913.477.7500 can tell you.

faqs: Trailer landing gear is punching into the asphalt at our K-7 warehouse. What's the fix?

Our site is in the Kansas River bottoms near 43rd Street. Does that change how the pavement gets built?

It can. The USDA soil survey maps the ground at Heartland Logistics Park and Westlink as Eudora and Bismarckgrove silt loams. Does cutting into the curb change the permit for a Shawnee driveway job?

Restoration has to be finished before the final inspection, so we close out the curb and yard work before we call it in. Rules change, so we go over them with Shawnee again when we write the proposal.
We're in Perimeter Park near 83rd and K-7. Can we fix our lot in phases instead of all at once?

Can our parking lot drain out through the driveway in Gardner?

Does the type of curb on my Gardner street change how a driveway approach is built?

faqs: Who has to fix a broken public sidewalk in front of a Leavenworth property?

Kansas law makes the owner of the abutting property responsible for keeping the sidewalk in repair, and it lets a city make the repair and assess the cost back to that property. Leavenworth also runs a cost-share program for replacing existing sidewalks or building new ones that are not part of a new subdivision or new building construction. Timing matters, because the owner has to ask to participate in writing before any work starts. A building permit and a city inspection come next, and once the work is done the owner submits the bill for reimbursement. The program does not cover brick sidewalks, and the city's share is set in its program guidelines, so we confirm the current figure with Public Works before we write your proposal.
What does Leavenworth require when a driveway approach is replaced?

The city requires a permit for any driveway approach or sidewalk in the public right-of-way, and the application goes to the Inspections Department with a site plan showing property lines and setbacks. Its infrastructure manual calls for at least 6 inches of concrete, with the old approach saw-cut full depth before it comes out and a half-inch pre-molded expansion joint at the cut. Curb cut for the new approach gets replaced between the nearest construction joints, and the work can't block the flow of water in the gutter. On a curbed street the approach can't be wider than 30 feet including wings and flares, or the zoning limit if that is smaller. The new approach also has to be graded so a sidewalk crossing it meets accessibility rules, and the city inspects the work before the pour.
Can a sidewalk repair in Leavenworth turn into a new curb ramp?

It can. The city's infrastructure standards say work on or near a sidewalk and the curb next to it is reason to install a curb ramp if current PROWAG accessibility rules call for one. Repaired walks also have to match the existing width or 4 feet, whichever is greater, with line and grade brought into compliance as far as the site allows. On an older block where the corner sits on a slope, that can change the scope of what started as a small repair. Our estimators check the corner slopes and the route to the street before they put a number on paper.
What does the city require before a commercial lot or truck apron gets dug out in Leavenworth?

The city's infrastructure manual requires 811 utility locates before any digging, and it ties excavations to a Land Disturbance Permit under Section 18-91 of the city code. Jobs that disturb an acre or more also need a notice of intent permit and have to follow KDHE erosion-control guidelines. Any excavation under a paved surface or within 2 feet of one is backfilled with flowable fill, though the City Engineer may approve AB-3 rock compacted in 8-inch lifts. New commercial developments need a drainage plan that meets the city's stormwater guidelines too. On a working lot we phase the pours so part of the site stays open, and a faster-curing mix that costs more can cut the wait before traffic from about 7 days to 2 or 3.
